Tides happen because of the invisible pull of gravity, mainly from the moon, but also from the sun. Imagine the Earth as a giant ball covered in water, spinning slowly through space. The moon, though far away, has a strong gravitational grip on our planet. As it orbits Earth, its gravity tugs at the oceans, pulling the water toward it. This pull isn’t the same everywhere—on the side of Earth facing the moon, the water is pulled most strongly, creating a bulge. That’s where high tide forms.

But here’s the interesting part: there’s also a bulge on the opposite side of the Earth. Why? Because the moon’s gravity pulls the Earth itself more than it pulls the water on the far side. So while the Earth is being tugged toward the moon, the water on the far side lags behind, creating a second bulge. These two bulges—on the near and far sides—are the high tides.

As Earth rotates on its axis once every 24 hours, different parts of the planet pass through these bulges. When a coastline moves into one of the bulges, the water rises, and we experience high tide. As it rotates out, the water recedes, and low tide follows. This cycle repeats roughly every 12 hours and 25 minutes, which is why most places have two high tides and two low tides each day.

The sun also plays a role, though it’s less powerful because it’s much farther away. When the sun, moon, and Earth line up—during new and full moons—their combined gravity creates extra strong tides called spring tides. When the sun and moon pull at right angles, their forces partially cancel, leading to weaker tides known as neap tides.

So tides are a dance between Earth’s rotation and the gravitational tugs of the moon and sun. It’s a quiet, rhythmic motion that shapes coastlines, guides sailors, and reminds us how deeply connected we are to the rhythms of the cosmos.
